summary: STRIDE: Junior Protocol is a free web game that trains kids aged 7 to 12 to run an outpost on Mars or the Moon. Players manage four limited resources (water, battery, shielding and mission time) across 4-day missions set in 8 real Argentine landscapes that scientists use as planetary analogs. Every day brings an event, like a sandstorm or a solar radiation spike, and a decision with visible consequences. Live NASA DONKI space weather makes shielding more expensive when the real Sun is active, and every event teaches a verified fact from NASA missions. It turns abstract space data into choices kids can feel, in Spanish and English, on any phone or computer.
details:
What it does. Kids pick a site on a live satellite radar: 4 Mars analogs in the Puna of Catamarca (Campo de Piedra Pómez, Antofagasta de la Sierra, Salar del Hombre Muerto, Carachi Pampa) or 4 Moon analogs in Chubut, Chaco and Neuquén (Bajada del Diablo, Bajo Hondo, Campo del Cielo, Barda Negra). Each mission lasts 4 days. Every day opens with a short cinematic of a real hazard, then the player makes one decision. Each option spends resources differently; risky plays are cheaper if they succeed but must be decided in seconds. The suit also consumes life support every day, so resources never cover everything. If any resource hits zero, the mission fails.

How it uses real data. The game queries NASA DONKI for solar flares, coronal mass ejections and geomagnetic storms from the last 60 days; the stronger the real event, the more shielding costs (up to +30%). When water or battery become critical, the game shows real astronaut health findings from NASA OSDR research such as the Twins Study. All 32 events include a verified fact from NASA missions (Viking, Curiosity, LRO, Apollo, Phoenix, MRO) or CONAE’s SAOCOM radar, compared with the Argentine site. Skies follow the science: butterscotch daytime and blue sunsets on Mars, a black sky on the airless Moon.

Learning design. PUNI, a robot sidekick, gives hints but never decides. After each mission players earn badges, join a leaderboard, keep what they learned in a Logbook and can download a Junior Astronaut certificate. Three difficulty levels (junior, senior, commander) were calibrated by simulating every possible path through all 8 missions: good choices always win, even under the worst real space weather, while random play loses often.

Why it matters. Space data is public but reaches kids as disconnected numbers. STRIDE connects a real solar storm to a concrete decision, and shows that places to study other worlds exist close to home.

Tools. Next.js, React, TypeScript, Three.js, Leaflet with Esri World Imagery, Supabase and Vercel. Background music was generated with Suno (AI), as credited in the game. Claude (AI) assisted with coding, testing and English translation.
